newsitem.title: RWANDA: FEATURE-Staging of "Hamlet" stirs controversy in Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Staging of "Hamlet" stirs controversy in Rwanda.

text.p: Staging William Shakespeare's "Hamlet" in Rwanda with a cast including war crimes tribunal staff is setting backers and critics musing anew on death and revenge.
Two years after the genocide of up to one million Rwandans, the first production of "Hamlet" in Kigali has met some opposition, particularly from zealous customs officers.
"We had a number of props, three rapiers and a dagger, which had come in from Chicago, and which seem to have been blocked at customs at the airport," says the tragedy's director, Joshua Walker.
But Walker, an amateur actor who works at the international genocide tribunal's office in the capital Kigali, is undeterred. "Most of the props got through. We've got the false beards," he says.

"Hamlet", with a handful of Rwandans in the cast, opens in Kigali on September 19 with seats costing 5,000 local francs ($13) each. Proceeds go to an orphanage for children whose parents were slaughtered in the genocide.
"We basically had the idea because we had been studying genocide and we wanted to understand it," said Walker.
"There is a spiritual side too. What the play is actually about is to speak the truth about what happened here, about ambition and corruption gone awry."

Hutu troops, militiamen and mobs butchered members of the Tutsi minority and moderates of the Hutu majority, falsely portraying the genocide as a popular reaction to the April 6, 1994, assassination of Hutu President Juvenal Habyarimana.
Much of the funding for "Hamlet" comes from the U.S. embassy, which sees the tragedy as a lesson for Rwanda.
"It is a Rwandan and American production. It is a great play and there is a great shortage of theatre here," says Alice Lemaistre, press and cultural attache at the embassy.
"The question in the play of whether revenge is a sacred duty or not is important. The play demonstrates it is not."

More than 80,000 people accused of involvement in the 1994 genocide are packed into Rwanda's prisons and lock-ups. The government says it is determined to put them on trial and wants the organisers of the mass slaughter to face the death penalty.
Tens of thousands of bodies remain hidden in mass graves across the hills and valleys of Rwanda. Thousands more have been exhumed and put on public display as memorials to the carnage.
Walker however says the skull which appears on stage in the "Alas! poor Yorick" scene was made specially for the play.

"I think Shakespeare said it right, in the words of Hamlet," Walker says. "'And let me speak to the yet unknowing world, how these things came about. So shall you hear of carnal bloody and unnatural acts, of accidental judgment and casual slaughter.'"
Philip Gourevitch, a writer with the New Yorker magazine who is visiting Rwanda, is a critic of the "Hamlet" project.

Asked for his reaction to Hamlet's quote by Walker, he says: "The world was not unknowing about the Rwandan genocide, it was indifferent. And the killing was not accidental or casual but precisely the opposite."
"Hamlet's a top play, but the grandiose attempts to equate it with Rwanda reflects a shocking and dilettantish naivete about what actually happened in this country," adds Gourevitch.

"To compare the story of one Danish prince's existential crisis following the murder of his father by his mother's lover with the systematic, state-sponsored extermination of one million Africans is utterly obscene."
Hamlet is played by another tribunal official, American Gregory Gordon. Ophelia on alternate nights is Rebeka Martensen of the U.N. refugee agency and Vicky White, an American aid worker.
The king is tribunal investigator Steve Myall, formerly of the police criminal investigation department in Essex, England.
"I like to think that perhaps there's a similarity between Ophelia floating down the river and...bodies floating in the Nyabarongo (river)," says Walker.
Hutu killers tossed many of the bodies of the Tutsi men, women and children they slaughtered into Rwanda's rivers. They also threw in live victims with their hands and legs bound.
Following Kigali, the play moves to southern Rwanda and the 1,400-seat theatre at the University of Butare, still in ruins since being wrecked during the genocide and three months of civil war.
Technical advice and assistance is being given by Hilary Mack-Austin, artistic director of the Chicago Actors Ensemble.
The English-language play also has a cultural edge in Rwanda, which was strongly francophone before the victory of Tutsi rebels -- many of them English-speaking -- who stopped the genocide.
"Hamlet" will be staged at the French Cultural Centre in the Rwandan capital because there are no other suitable facilities.
($1 = 385 francs)
